problem_motivation.content: There is a lack of understanding regarding the oxidation mechanisms of RHEAs, particularly concerning long-term exposure beyond 48 hours.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date

problem_motivation.content: There is a need for materials with higher temperature capabilities beyond Ni-based superalloys, and specifically a need to understand long-term oxidation behavior and mechanisms in Refractory High-Entropy Alloys (RHEAs).
problem_motivation.evidence_span: As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities.

problem_motivation.content: The oxidation mechanism for low mass gain in AlCrMoTaTi RHEA remains unclear due to lack of detailed microstructure characterization.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: this extremely low mass gain at 1000 °C was claimed to be due to formation of Al 2 O 3 layer on the alloy surface, however, the associated oxidation mechanism was not clear since there was no detailed microstructure characterization.

problem_motivation.content: Previous studies are limited to short durations (48 hours) with no indication of long-term effectiveness of protective oxide layers.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Furthermore, these previous oxidation studies were conducted for only up to 48 hours, and there was no indication whether this Al 2 O 3 layer could still be effective after a longer exposure.

prior_approach.content: Senkov et al. reported on the oxidation of CrMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr alloy, noting severe spallation and high mass gain.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Oxidation of CrMo 0.5 NbTa 0.5 TiZr alloy was firstly reported by Senkov et al . [11] , which showed severe spallation of oxide layer and about 120 mg/cm 2 of mass gain after 100 hours of oxidation at 1000 °C.

prior_approach.content: Gorr et al. reported oxidation behavior of several RHEAs including AlCrMoTiW, AlCrMoNbTi, and Si-doped variants.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Gorr et al . [12] , [13] reported the oxidation behaviour of AlCrMoTiW, AlCrMoNbTi, and (AlCrMoNbTi) 0.99 Si 0.01 alloys.

prior_approach.content: Gorr et al. reported low mass gain for AlCrMoTaTi attributed to Al2O3 formation, though without detailed characterization.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The most recent study on the oxidation behaviour of AlCrMoTaTi reported by Gorr et al . [14] indicated a mass gain after 48 hours of oxidation at 1000 and 1100 °C was less than 1 and 3 mg/cm 2 , respectively; this extremely low mass gain at 1000 °C was claimed to be due to formation of Al 2 O 3 layer on the alloy surface

prior_approach.content: The NV1 alloy design was based on a CrMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr alloy previously proposed by Senkov et al.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The design of NV1 was based on CrMo 0.5 NbTa 0.5 TiZr alloy proposed by Senkov et al . [11] , [33]

prior_limitation.content: Existing reported oxidation behaviors of RHEAs are limited to short-term exposures of only up to 48 hours.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours

prior_limitation.content: The study of CrMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr by Senkov et al. showed severe degradation via oxide spallation.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Oxidation of CrMo 0.5 NbTa 0.5 TiZr alloy was firstly reported by Senkov et al . [11] , which showed severe spallation of oxide layer

prior_limitation.content: AlCrMoTiW failed to form a continuous oxide layer on the sample surface.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: For AlCrMoTiW, despite no formation of continuous oxide layer on a sample surface was observed

prior_limitation.content: Previous studies lacked detailed microstructure characterization to clarify oxidation mechanisms despite reported low mass gains.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: however, the associated oxidation mechanism was not clear since there was no detailed microstructure characterization.

prior_limitation.content: Previous studies were limited to short durations (48 hours) without evidence of long-term effectiveness.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Furthermore, these previous oxidation studies were conducted for only up to 48 hours

prior_limitation.content: Prior studies on RHEAs/RCCAs only tested up to 48 hours, which was insufficient to confirm long-term protection by Al2O3/Cr2O3 layers.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: However, the testing duration in these previous studies was within 48 hours, which was not long enough to confirm whether these RHEAs/RCCAs were really protected by Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 .

prior_limitation.content: Prior reports suggested Al activity values indicating protective Al2O3 formation, but this study found no such layer formed despite higher Al activity.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Obviously, NV1 alloy possessed much higher Al activities at both temperature than those of AlCrMoTaTi alloy, which was claimed to be able to form a protective Al 2 O 3 layer, but no protective Al 2 O 3 layer was found on NV1 alloy in present study.

causal_claim.content: The formation of a protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer at 1100 °C resulted in two distinct parabolic dependences in the mass gain curve.
causal_claim.evidence_span: mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer

mechanism_principle.content: The exponential dependence of weight gain observed at 1000 °C is caused by the inability to form a dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours

mechanism_principle.content: The exponential weight gain behavior at 1000 C is explained by the continuous growth of the external oxide layer and nitridation depth.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This analysis indicates that exponential oxidation weight gain behaviour at 1000 °C was mainly attributed by a steady increase in the oxide layer formed externally and the nitridation depth.

mechanism_principle.content: The increased Al content and reduced Cr content in the oxide layer at 1100°C are caused by enhanced Al diffusion and substitution of Cr by Al in the lattice.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The increased Al content in CrTaO 4 -based oxide at 1100 °C reflected the fact that the kinetics for Al was enhanced when the temperature was increased from 1000 °C to 1100 °C, allowing more prominent outward diffusion of Al into the CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer. The reduced Cr content was most likely caused by substitution of Cr atoms with Al atoms in CrTaO 4 lattice since both Al and Cr could form rutile-type AlTaO 4 and CrTaO 4 .

mechanism_principle.content: The non-stoichiometric nature of the CrTaO4-based oxide suppresses detrimental oxides by accommodating metallic atoms within the CrTaO4 lattice.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Such property potentially suppressed the formation of detrimental oxides, such as Nb 2 O 5 and TiO 2 , since the metallic atoms of these oxides were accommodated by CrTaO 4 instead of forming their individual oxides.

mechanism_principle.content: MoO3 evaporation creates paths for oxygen ingress, accelerating oxidation of underlying regions despite the net weight gain remaining positive.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The evaporation of MoO 3 created additional paths for oxygen ingress, accelerating the oxidation of the regions beneath the oxide layer. But since MoO 3 evaporated only from ~2 μm-thick OL/IOD interface, the weight loss resulting from MoO 3 evaporation shall be neglectable comparing to the weight gain from the accelerated oxidation of the other regions.

hypothesis_statement.content: The work is proposed to provide insights on developing RHEAs to withstand long-term oxidation at elevated temperatures.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: This work can also provide insights on how to further develop RHEA to withstand long term oxidation at elevated temperatures

hypothesis_statement.content: It is proposed that reduced Ti content in NV1 promotes CrTaO4 formation, enhancing oxidation resistance compared to alloys with more Ti.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Since CrTaO 4 layer played a major role in reducing the oxidation of NV1 alloy, it is very likely that the reduced Ti content of NV1 alloy promoted the formation of CrTaO 4 layer, leading to enhanced oxidation resistance at 1100 °C.

hypothesis_statement.content: It is hypothesized that the growth of protective Al2O3 or Cr2O3 layers may be hindered by the presence of CrTaO4-based oxide.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: However, it is also possible that the growth of a protective Al 2 O 3 or Cr 2 O 3 layer was hindered by prominent CrTaO 4 -based oxide presence.

evidence_result.content: The measured weight gain after 200 hours at 1100 °C was 4.03 mg/cm2.
evidence_result.evidence_span: the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2

evidence_result.content: Measured oxidation mass gain of 6.53 mg/cm2 after 200 hours at 1000 C.
evidence_result.evidence_span: After 200 hours of oxidation, the mass gain was 6.53 mg/cm 2 .

evidence_result.content: XRD analysis identified three distinct oxide phases on the surface after oxidation.
evidence_result.evidence_span: XRD analysis on the oxidised sample surface revealed 3 different oxides existing in the oxide layer (Fig. 3 ): CrTaO 4 , Al 2 O 3 , and Cr 2 O 3 .

evidence_result.content: Measured lattice constants of the CrTaO4-based oxide showing slight contraction compared to pure CrTaO4.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The detected CrTaO 4 -based oxide had lattice constants of a = 4.625 Å and c = 3.007 Å that were 0.37% less in a axis and 0.43% less in c axis comparing to those of pure CrTaO 4 ( a = 4.642 Å, c = 3.020 Å provided by PDF No. 39–1428).

evidence_result.content: EDS mapping confirmed the absence of a continuous protective Al2O3 or Cr2O3 layer on the surface.
evidence_result.evidence_span: According to EDS mapping, neither continuous Al 2 O 3 nor Cr 2 O 3 layer was found on the alloy surface after 200 hours of oxidation at 1000 °C.

evidence_result.content: Measured oxidation mass gain of 4.03 mg/cm2 after 200 hours at 1100 C.
evidence_result.evidence_span: after 200 hours of oxidation, the mass gain per initial surface area was 4.03 mg/cm 2

evidence_result.content: The weight gain of the alloy after 200 hours at 1100°C was measured as 4.03 mg/cm2.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The weight gain of the alloy at 1100 °C after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2

constraint.content: Long-term testing (100+ hours) is required to properly study protective oxide scales in RHEAs, unlike the short durations in prior studies.
constraint.evidence_span: To study protective oxide scale, testing duration of 100 hours or beyond is necessary [27] – [29] .

constraint.content: The scanning rate for XRD was constrained to 10 degrees per minute.
constraint.evidence_span: with a scanning rate of 10° per minute

constraint.content: TGA tests were constrained to a weight recording interval of 0.04 hours.
constraint.evidence_span: the weight change was recorded automatically every 0.04 hour

constraint.content: The isothermal oxidation test required a minimum repetition of 4 times per condition to ensure consistency.
constraint.evidence_span: The isothermal oxidation test was repeated at least 4 times for each testing condition

contradiction.content: Oxidation behavior at 1100 C differs from 1000 C, showing three stages instead of exponential growth and different growth profiles for OL and IND.
contradiction.evidence_span: Figure 5 shows the length of OL, IOD, and IND versus time with respect to the oxidation weight gain at 1100 °C. Unlike the result of 1000 °C, only IND length increased drastically during the oxidation at 1100 °C, while OL and IOD length increments were moderate.
